lead: A topology is the pattern in which links join nodes. A node is any device that sends or receives: a computer, switch, router or printer. A link is the cable or wireless channel between two nodes. The physical topology is where the cables run; the logical topology is the path a frame takes. Each pattern trades cable and port cost against fault tolerance and easy growth. A lab may use a star, a campus a star-bus, a bank a partial mesh. The pattern decides how a frame travels, how many ports each device needs, and what happens when one cable or one device fails.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.2, to know which topology suits a LAN, a MAN and a WAN.

blocks.text: A full mesh joins every node to every other node. For the mesh formulas, n is the total number of nodes. A frame from A to B travels one link, directly. With n nodes, each node has a link to the other n − 1 nodes. Counting each cable at both ends gives n(n − 1) ends; divide by 2 because one cable serves both ends.

blocks.where: n is the total number of nodes; links is the number of cables in a full mesh.
n is the total number of nodes; each node needs one port for every other node.

blocks.text: Full mesh is the most fault tolerant. If one link fails, only that direct path is lost; traffic can often go another way. If one node fails, the rest still reach each other. Adding a node to a mesh of n nodes needs n new cables, one new port on each old node, and n ports on the new node; total ports grow as n², so growth is expensive. A partial mesh keeps some direct links and leaves the rest to indirect paths. WAN cores and data-centre spines often use partial mesh. Cost is high: links and ports grow about n².

A star has one central device, usually a switch, with one link to each node. A frame from PC1 to PC3 goes PC1 → switch → PC3, two link hops. With n end nodes (the switch is not counted in n), a star needs n cables and n ports on the central device; each node needs one port. Cost grows linearly. If one cable fails, only that node drops. If the central device fails, the whole star drops: a single point of failure. Adding a node needs one cable and one free central port. The switch itself is in Chapter 1.8.

A bus uses one backbone cable with taps. A frame travels both directions along the backbone; every node hears it. For bus formulas, n means end nodes only; the backbone is not counted. A bus needs one backbone cable and one tap per node; a node needs one port. It is cheap for few nodes. A break in the backbone usually stops all transmission on the bus, because the cut end reflects signals; splitting it into working parts needs repeaters, bridges or separate segments. Adding a node means cutting or tapping the cable, often disrupting service. Access rules for a shared bus are in Unit 3.

A ring joins nodes in a closed loop. Each node has two ports, one to each neighbour; a frame travels around the ring until it reaches the destination. For ring formulas, n means end nodes only. A simple ring needs n links and 2 ports per node. One cable cut breaks the loop; a dual ring can survive one cut. Adding a node means opening the ring and inserting two links. Access methods are in Unit 3.

A tree is a hierarchy of stars: leaves join a switch, switches join a backbone. A frame climbs to a common parent and down. The root or backbone link is a shared risk. Real campuses use a hybrid: a star-bus or star-ring, meaning stars joined by a bus or ring backbone.

blocks.text: Cost follows links and ports: mesh grows as n²; star, bus and ring grow linearly. Choose by cost and risk. An eight-PC lab suits a star: cheap and easy. A bank WAN suits a partial mesh between key sites. A factory bus suits one cable along machines. A metro ring suits a dual ring that survives one cut. A campus suits a star-bus or star-ring.

examples.question: A college lab has 8 computers. Compare a full mesh and a star. Each cable run is 20 m and cable costs ₹30 per metre. The star uses one switch. Find (a) mesh cables, (b) ports per mesh computer, (c) star cables, (d) star switch ports, (e) cable length and cost for each.
steps: Mesh ports per computer = n − 1 = 8 − 1 = 7 ports.
Star switch ports = n = 8 ports; each computer uses 1 port.
One cable run = 20 m. Star cable length = 8 × 20 = 160 m. Cost = 160 × ₹30 = ₹4,800.
Failure: mesh survives any single cable cut; star dies if the switch fails, and one cable cut isolates one PC.
examples.answer: Mesh needs 28 cables and 7 ports per computer; star needs 8 cables, 8 switch ports and 1 port per computer. Star cable costs ₹4,800; mesh cable costs ₹16,800.

traps: Writing n(n − 1) links for a full mesh and forgetting the ÷ 2; the cost then comes out exactly double.
Swapping links and ports: a full mesh has n(n − 1)/2 cables, but n − 1 ports per node, not n(n − 1)/2 ports per node.
Calling a star fault tolerant because each cable is separate: the centre is a single point of failure.
Treating physical and logical topology as the same: a star-wired LAN may run a logical bus or ring.

Assuming a bus cable break only affects part of the network: on a plain bus with one terminated backbone cable, a break or fault usually stops all transmission on the whole bus, because the cut end reflects signals. Splitting the bus into working parts needs repeaters, bridges or separate segments.

quiz.q: Define topology. What is a node and a link?
quiz.a: A topology is the pattern in which links join nodes. A node is a device that sends or receives data. A link is the cable or wireless channel between two nodes.

quiz.q: Why is a full mesh fault tolerant but costly?
quiz.a: Every pair has a direct link, so one cut leaves other paths and one node failure does not stop the rest. Cost is high because links grow as n(n − 1)/2 and each node needs n − 1 ports.

quiz.q: A full mesh has 6 nodes. Find the number of links and the ports per node.
quiz.a: links = 6 × 5 / 2 = 15 cables. ports per node = 6 − 1 = 5 ports.

quiz.q: A star has 10 PCs and one switch. Find the cables, switch ports and ports per PC.
quiz.a: Cables = 10. Switch ports = 10. Ports per PC = 1.

quiz.q: A lab needs 8 PCs. Give one reason to choose a star over a full mesh and one reason to choose a mesh over a star.
quiz.a: Star: 8 cables and 8 switch ports, far cheaper than 28 mesh cables and 7 ports per PC. Mesh: a single cable cut cannot separate the network, while a star dies if the switch fails.

quiz.q: A campus uses a star-bus. Explain what fails if one leaf cable breaks and if the bus backbone breaks.
quiz.a: A leaf cable break drops only that leaf node; the rest of its star still works. A bus backbone break usually stops the whole bus segment, because the cut end reflects signals; it splits into working parts only if repeaters or bridges are used.

beyond: Not for the exam. Data centres now use leaf-spine and fat-tree topologies, which are partial-mesh designs built from many equal-cost paths. Cloud providers describe regions and availability zones as logical topologies over physical fibre. Software-defined networking lets a controller choose logical paths without rewiring. Search terms: leaf-spine, fat-tree, Clos network, network topology graph.
